newsitem.title: USA: Germany will meet strict EMU targets, says Waigel.
newsitem.headline: Germany will meet strict EMU targets, says Waigel.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Sunday that Germany would strictly meet criteria needed to join European monetary union (EMU), brushing aside recent reports of fiscal worries in Bonn.

Speaking to a news briefing ahead of the semi-annual Group of Seven (G7) meetings, Waigel said Germany would cut its budget deficit to below the three percent of gross domestic product level mandated by the Maastricht Treaty for nations wanting to join EMU.
"The government stands by its 2.9 percent budget forecast for this year," Waigel said. Germany's budget deficit stood at 3.8 percent of GDP in 1996.
The finance minister added that Bonn was ready to take additional measures to ensure it met the Maastricht criteria, but did not indicate specifically how this would be done.
Waigel's comments follow a spate of reports about Germany and other nations' efforts to qualify for monetary union.
The International Monetary Fund forecast last week that Germany would only be able to cut its deficit to 3.3 percent of GDP.
Germany's six top economic institutes said, meanwhile, that the deficit would fall to 3.2 percent, although they group added that 3.0 percent was still possible.
Waigel's comments were the latest sign of hope that European nations will cut their deficits sufficiently to enable a launch of monetary union on schedule on January 1, 1999.

Massimo Russo, special adviser to International Monetary Fund managing director Michael Camdessus, said on Saturday that one of the nations having the most difficult time qualifying for EMU, Italy, could make the grade in 1998.

Although the IMF forecast Italy's deficit to be 3.3 percent of GDP this year and 4.1 percent in 1998, Russo said Rome could still undertake additional budget measures to trim its deficit to the three percent EMU hurdle.
"There is still time to bring the deficit below three percent in 1998," he said.
At the centre of the drive to slash deficits is a worry that failure to launch EMU on time would be dangerous to the project as a whole.
"We at the IMF believe a delay ... would lead to substantial dangers," Russo said, adding the project could be shelved for some time if it does not start in 1999.
